title: Saul Meets Jesus
lead: The greatest opponent can become one of God’s most important instruments.
questions: Who is your Saul, the person you have stopped praying for, and to whom is God sending you today as an Ananias?
Can you talk about your own past the way Paul did: without whitewashing it, and with mercy as the punch line?
When someone we used to be afraid of walks into our church, what is your first word: “brother,” or “we’ll see”?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: In the previous part we looked at the birth of the church; today we meet the man who set out to wipe it out. Saul “was still breathing out murderous threats against the disciples of the Lord,” but he is no thug: he is a superbly educated Pharisee, a student of Gamaliel, convinced he is defending God. He travels to Damascus with official letters authorizing him to arrest “men or women,” because from the very beginning they were an important part of the church. The movement itself is called “the Way” here – not yet a doctrine, just a way of life. Saul, set on wiping out those faithful to God, is no exception. The most dangerous things in the history of religion have been done by devout people with Scripture on their lips. Zeal is no proof that you are right. Sometimes it only measures your momentum.

Near Damascus the student of Gamaliel is stopped by a light. Then comes a question: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” Me. After all, Saul had been persecuting people, but the risen Lord feels every blow aimed at His own. Paul’s entire later theology of the church as the body of Christ was born in that one sentence. Whenever we wound any of His people, we touch the apple of His eye. Saul lost his sight, and there is a kind of parable in that: the official with the seals is led into the city by the hand. Three days of darkness, fasting, and the prayer of a man whose picture of the world had fallen apart. There are moments of blindness like that after which we see better than through years of perfect eyesight.

God sends to Saul not an apostle but an ordinary disciple. Ananias is honestly afraid: Lord, this man came here to arrest us. But he goes, lays his hands on the persecutor, and says, “Brother Saul.” The first word with which the church addressed its tormentor was a welcome into the family. God accomplished the conversion on the road, but He needed a person to hold out a hand. Without people like Ananias, no Damascus road has a sequel. God accepted Saul in the middle of his error, not after he had reformed, and He did not break his temperament; He turned it around. The momentum of hatred became the driving force of mission.

This story forbids us to write people off. Pray for your Saul, the one who “will never change.” And once God has turned him around, be an Ananias. Let your first word be “brother,” before you say anything else.

In the previous part we looked at the birth of the church. Today we meet the man who set out to wipe that church out. Luke introduces him without mincing words: Saul “was still breathing out murderous threats against the disciples of the Lord.” He is not a thug or a cynic. He is a superbly educated Pharisee, brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel,” a man who would later write of his own past that as to zeal he persecuted the church, and as to righteousness in the law he was faultless. Saul did not destroy Jesus’ disciples against his conscience; he did it in keeping with it. He was dead certain he was defending God. That is the first and most uncomfortable lesson of this story: the most dangerous things in the history of religion have been done by deeply devout people, with a sense of duty and Scripture on their lips. Zeal is no proof that you are right. Sometimes it only measures your momentum.

sections.heading: Letters in His Bag
paragraphs: It is worth looking at the bureaucracy behind this persecution. Saul had to go to the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus. These documents authorized arrests outside Judea and the transport of prisoners to Jerusalem. The warrant covered “men or women,” which lets slip, almost in passing, how important a role women played in the young church from the very beginning – nobody bothers arresting extras. The movement itself was called “the Way.” It is the oldest name for Christianity we know: not yet a doctrine, not an institution, but a way of life. So Saul sets out with documents in his bag to block that Way. He has more than a hundred and thirty miles to walk and plenty of time to think. At the end of that road he meets not a victim but Someone who had been waiting for him in particular for a long time.

sections.heading: Why Do You Persecute Me?
paragraphs: Right outside Damascus a light from heaven flashes around him. He falls to the ground and hears a question: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” Hidden in that question is a theology Saul was not ready for. He had not been oppressing Christ, after all. Jesus was dead, or so Saul believed. He had been persecuting people. He had dragged men and women out of their homes and given his approval to Stephen’s death – later he himself admitted that he had voted for death sentences against believers. Yet the voice from heaven says “Me.” The risen Lord identifies with His people so literally that a blow aimed at the least of them hurts Him Himself. Saul asks the only sensible question that can be asked in that situation: “Who are You, Lord?” He will hear an answer that turns his world upside down: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” Paul’s entire later theology of the church as the body of Christ was born in that one sentence, spoken to a persecutor lying in the dust. Whoever touches the community of believers touches Christ. That is worth remembering in the other direction too, inside the church. If we wound any of His people, even the least of them, even the one we think is most in the wrong, we touch the apple of His eye.

sections.heading: Three Days of Darkness
paragraphs: Saul lost his sight, and there is a kind of parable in that, when an authority bearing official seals is led into the city by the hand like a child. For three days he sees nothing, eats nothing, drinks nothing. This darkness is not a punishment – it is a place of transformation, a kind of tomb from which someone else will come out. Surrounded by it, Saul does something God notes with tenderness: “he is praying.” Saul’s prayers had been known to every synagogue – he had been a devout man since childhood. But this is a different prayer. For the first time a broken man comes to God, a man whose whole picture of the world has fallen apart. There are three days of darkness like that in life, after which we see better than through years of perfect eyesight.

sections.heading: Brother Saul
paragraphs: Then a hero steps onto the stage who is rarely mentioned in sermons: Ananias, “a disciple” in Damascus. Not an apostle, not a prophet, just an ordinary believer in the city where an inquisitor with warrants was on his way. The Lord tells him to go to Straight Street and lay his hands on Saul of Tarsus. Ananias’s answer is wonderfully honest – he explains to God that this man has done a great deal of harm and has come to Damascus to arrest the faithful. Ananias doesn’t fake a courage he doesn’t have. God doesn’t mock his fear; instead He shows him a piece of His plan: “Go!” And then: “This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings.” Soon afterward comes one of the most beautiful scenes in the whole book of Acts. Ananias walks into the house, lays his hands on the man who came to put him in prison, and says, “Brother Saul.” Brother. The church’s first word to its persecutor was a welcome into the family. Not “prove yourself first,” not “we’ll see whether you can be trusted,” but: “Brother Saul… the Lord Jesus… has sent me so that you may see again.” Something like scales falls from Saul’s eyes; he is baptized, eats, and regains his strength. God accomplished the conversion on the road, but He still needed a person to hold out a hand to the convert and call him brother. Without people like Ananias, no Damascus road has a sequel.

sections.heading: An Instrument with a Price
paragraphs: Notice what God says about Saul’s future: “This man is My chosen instrument,” and right after that: “I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.” The calling here is not a reward or a certificate of merit, but a task with a price built in. The former persecutor will be persecuted from now on; the author of letters authorizing arrests will write letters from prison. The first installment of that price comes soon: right there in Damascus, the city he had come to as a hunter, he becomes the hunted and has to escape by night, lowered in a basket through an opening in the wall. The man who had ridden in on the main road with the high priest’s seals leaves the city in a cargo basket, like smuggled goods. Yet he will never remember that escape with shame. Years later he will describe it himself, once he has learned that God’s power likes to be perfected in weakness. It is also worth stressing that the Lord accepted Saul as he was, in the middle of his greatest mistake, not after he had reformed. He did not wait for him to do penance, think things over, and mellow. He stopped him at the full momentum of his hatred and turned his zeal toward mission. The same energy that drove him to Damascus with arrest warrants would later carry him across half the empire with the gospel. God doesn’t break people’s temperaments. He turns them around.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: Three main lessons are hidden in this story. First, we must not write off the Sauls of today, people of whom it is said, “That one will never change.” It may be a militant opponent of faith in your family, someone who wounds the church or wounds you. In spite of everything, we are to show such a person love. The greatest enemy the church ever had became its greatest missionary, and interceding for today’s Sauls is one of the most biblical prayers we know. Second, you can come to God with any past. That past can become our strongest testimony, just as it did for Paul. To the end of his life he remembered who he had been and kept saying that he had been shown mercy. The third lesson concerns us as a community – we are to be people like Ananias. We have to ask ourselves whether, when a person with a history we used to fear walks into our church, our first word is “brother,” “sister,” or rather “we’ll see.” God took care of His part of the business with Saul out on the road. Our part begins on Straight Street. We are to go, lay on our hands, and call someone a brother whom yesterday we were afraid of. Everything hung on that one word: whether the converted Saul would become Paul, or remain a lonely, blind man in a stranger’s house.
